content: Cardiovascular technologists and technicians assist physicians in diagnosing and treating conditions related to the heart (cardiac) and blood vessels (peripheral vascular). Cardiovascular technologists may specialize in one of three areas: invasive cardiology, echocardiography, or vascular technology. Technicians who specialize in electrocardiograms (EKGs), stress testing, and Holter monitoring are referred to as cardiographic technicians or EKG technicians. Cardiovascular technologists specializing in invasive procedures are known as invasive cardiovascular technologists. They assist physicians during cardiac catheterization procedures, where a small tube (catheter) is inserted into a patient’s artery, typically from the groin, and guided to the heart. This procedure helps determine if there are blockages in the blood vessels supplying the heart muscle and can also diagnose other cardiac issues. In some cases, the procedure may involve balloon angioplasty, which treats blockages in blood vessels or heart valves without requiring open-heart surgery. Invasive cardiovascular technologists assist physicians by threading a catheter with a balloon at its tip to the site of the obstruction. These technologists prepare patients for cardiac catheterization and balloon angioplasty by positioning them on an examination table, shaving and cleaning the area near the groin, and administering local anesthesia. During the procedure, they monitor the patient’s blood pressure and heart rate using EKG equipment and alert the physician to any abnormalities. They may also assist during open-heart surgery and the insertion of pacemakers or stents, which are used to open blocked arteries or major blood vessels. Technologists who use ultrasound to examine the heart’s chambers, valves, and vessels are called cardiac sonographers. They operate ultrasound equipment to create images known as echocardiograms. These tests can be performed while the patient is at rest or during physical activity. In some cases, cardiac sonographers administer medications to simulate physical activity and assess heart function. They may also assist physicians in performing transesophageal echocardiography, a procedure that involves inserting a tube into the patient’s esophagus to obtain detailed ultrasound images of the heart. Vascular technologists, also known as vascular specialists or vascular sonographers, assist physicians in diagnosing disorders affecting blood circulation. They take medical histories, evaluate pulses, and assess blood flow in arteries and veins by listening for abnormalities in vascular sounds. They perform noninvasive procedures using ultrasound equipment to record vascular data, such as blood flow, blood pressure, limb volume changes, oxygen saturation, and circulation in the brain, peripheral areas, and abdomen. Many of these tests are conducted during or immediately after surgery. EKG technicians, who specialize in obtaining electrocardiograms, attach electrodes to the patient’s chest, arms, and legs to trace the electrical impulses transmitted by the heart. They operate EKG machines to obtain readings, which are printed for interpretation by a physician. This test is often performed before surgery or as part of routine physical exams, particularly for middle-aged individuals or those with a history of cardiovascular issues. EKG technicians with advanced training may also perform Holter monitoring and stress testing. For Holter monitoring, technicians attach electrodes to the patient’s chest and connect them to a portable EKG monitor worn on the patient’s belt. After 24 or more hours of normal activity, the technician removes the monitor, retrieves the recorded data, and checks the quality of the impulses on an electronic screen. The data is then printed for physician analysis, which helps diagnose heart rhythm abnormalities or pacemaker issues. During treadmill stress tests, EKG technicians document the patient’s medical history, explain the procedure, connect the patient to an EKG monitor, and obtain baseline readings and resting blood pressure. They then monitor the heart’s performance as the patient walks on a treadmill, gradually increasing the treadmill’s speed to observe the effects of exertion. Like vascular technologists and cardiac sonographers, EKG technicians performing these tests are classified as “noninvasive” technicians.
